title: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party
description: The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.The Jewish body, which is the la
body: The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.The Jewish body, which is the largest in the UK, was responding to the "Zionism is racism" policy motion passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.Board of Deputies president Phil Rosenberg said a vote passed by 118 votes to one to declare that the Greens had, "by adopting an antisemitic platform, become a racist party".A spokesman for the Greens insisted the party does not discriminate against people who hold Zionist views and said it rejected the Board of Deputies' "characterisation of this motion and our party".They added the decision "will not stop us from speaking out against the genocide in Gaza and pushing for stronger sanctions against the Israeli government and its leaders". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.The motion passed by the Board of Deputies urged other parties not to do deals with the Greens unless they rejected the policy.Forming coalition deals with Greens at local or national level would be "failing to take antisemitism with the requisite seriousness", it said, unless the party's local leadership have rejected the policy and committed to overturn it.Labour has already issued an ultimatum to local Green groups it is currently in coalition with, telling them to disown the motion or lose the party's support.Rosenberg said: "By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly."No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist."The Green Party's policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organisations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political licence."The Green Party's leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and confronting the antisemitism it has legitimised."The motion backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, and opposition political parties. Responding when the Green motion was passed, the Board of Deputies and Jewish Leadership Council said in a joint statement that "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote on the motion as he left the conference early to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election which was held days later.He has since told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, he would not overturn the motion, which would be party policy until 2028.

schema.headline: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party

title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
description: Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning t
body: Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians  had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous"."We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close.Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.This was also the case outside booths in number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.

schema.headline: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement

title: Letter making claims about Meghan's father written by his ex-wife, BBC understands
description: A letter sent to the Metropolitan Police making a number of claims relating to the Duchess of Sussex's father was written by his ex-wife Roslyn Lovele
body: A letter sent to the Metropolitan Police making a number of claims relating to the Duchess of Sussex's father was written by his ex-wife Roslyn Loveless, the BBC understands.Meghan confirmed on Friday she had previously been informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father, Thomas Markle.On Saturday, the Met confirmed it received a letter relating to Markle in 2019, and it was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle, 82, had been found in his former home in the Philippines. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's half-siblings Samantha Markle and Thomas Markle Jr. Loveless divorced Markle in 1975 before he married the Duchess' mother Doria Ragland in 1979. Meghan was born in 1981 and is the only daughter of Markle and Ragland.In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Markle in a letter - sent while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated - that he would never meet his grandchildren.On Friday, Meghan's half-brother claimed to the Sun he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.He is reported to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".It is understood that he contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about the images in July. The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.Officials in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating allegations relating to Markle. They told the BBC on Friday that the Philippines' anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.Markle gave an interview to the Mail on Sunday in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denied sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.The Met Police has said it did not pass on the contents of the letter shared with the Sussexes to other law enforcement agencies. The force is now reviewing its handling of the matter.Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.

schema.headline: Letter making claims about Meghan's father written by his ex-wife, BBC understands

title: Opposition leader María Machado returns to Venezuela
description: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile."I am here. Wi
body: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile."I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail. In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro. The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands. She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil.""Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said.He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied. It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held. Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote.Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before her fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize.In the 2024 election, Machado's ally González ran in her place against Maduro.The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty. A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future"."We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added.Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe". "I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said.In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump. The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others".US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks. "The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X.He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy."

schema.headline: Opposition leader María Machado returns to Venezuela

title: Two men killed by falling trees as Storm Boelo leaves 90,000 properties without power
description: The Metropolitan Police were called to Dollis Road in Finchley at around 12:40 GMT to reports a tree had fallen onto a moving car, and the man was pro
body: The Metropolitan Police were called to Dollis Road in Finchley at around 12:40 GMT to reports a tree had fallen onto a moving car, and the man was pronounced dead at the scene.Chief Inspector Guy Ellwood, from the North West Command Unit, said: "This is a deeply tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the young man who lost his life."A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said it sent incident response officers, paramedics from its hazardous area response team, and a trauma team from London's Air Ambulance to the scene.Earlier, Police Scotland said a man died after being hit by a falling tree in southern  near Castle Douglas.During Storm Boelo and the earlier Storm Austen, which hit the UK on Friday, 838,700 properties across the country faced power cuts, according to the ENA.Wind gusts peaked on Sunday morning at 85mph in Machrihanish, in Argyll and Bute, and 84mph in both Stornoway in the Outer Hebrides, and Capel Curig in north Wales.An amber wind warning issued by the Met Office was in place until 21:00 on Sunday across Scotland and parts of northern England.A yellow warning that also covered other areas of the north of England, including Liverpool, Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield and Newcastle-upon-Tyne, as well as parts of the East and West Midlands and North Wales, also expired at 21:00.The Met Office urged people to "stay indoors as much as possible", adding: "If you do go out, try not to walk, or shelter, close to buildings and trees."The strongest gusts have continued to spread eastwards across the UK on Sunday.The towns of the Clyde coast in Scotland have been hit particularly hard by the severe weather. The main Skelmorlie to Largs road has been badly damaged and a number of businesses in Largs were flooded overnight on Saturday.In Gourock, a boat ended up on the side of the road and there have been reports of power being out in Girvan all throughout Sunday. In Dumbarton, on the north bank of the River Clyde, Muhammad Zubair Ashraf's mobile phone shop was flooded overnight. He estimated between £5,000 and £10,000 of damage was caused and said he was "heartbroken" at the scale of the losses.Travel has been affected across the country, with police in Scotland warning against unnecessary road journeys.Ferry services have been impacted, some flights to and from Belfast, Glasgow, Aberdeen and Dublin airports have been cancelled, and train services across the UK have faced disruption.

schema.headline: Two men killed by falling trees as Storm Boelo leaves 90,000 properties without power

title: Sharon Osbourne: 'I visit Ozzy's grave every day'
description: Image caption, Sharon Osbourne spoke to BBC News as the family prepares to release a film about Ozzy's final concert with Black SabbathByMusic corresp
body: Image caption, Sharon Osbourne spoke to BBC News as the family prepares to release a film about Ozzy's final concert with Black SabbathByMusic correspondentIt's been 15 months since Ozzy Osbourne died, at the age of 76, at his home in Buckinghamshire.Although he had suffered from health problems for years, including Parkinson's disease and a fractured vertebra, his death was a shock.Less than three weeks beforehand, he had been on stage in Birmingham, playing a triumphant farewell concert.After the show, he was on a high."He was just so, so happy," recalls his wife Sharon."He was online, going through the reviews and saying, 'There's something terribly wrong', and I'm like, 'Why?'"He goes, 'I didn't get slagged by anybody. Why are people being nice to me?'"And I'm like, 'Because they like you'."On the morning he died, Ozzy had woken up early and gone downstairs for his usual morning workout. Shortly afterwards, he had a heart attack. An air ambulance was called and paramedics tried to save him. But it was too late."I was asleep," says Sharon."We'd spoken in the night. Ozzy had woken in the night and he asked me to kiss him twice, and I did."And then he said, 'Hold me, hold me tight,' and I did."And then the next thing I know, it's early in the morning, and someone comes rushing into the room saying, 'Come down now'."I ran down, and that was it."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sharon and Ozzy Osbourne, pictured in 2017 after renewing their wedding vows The grief, she says, will never leave."You've lost the love of your life, so you don't just wake up and go, 'I'm fine now. I'm cured'."You never get over it. But you learn to live with it, and that's what I'm trying to do. So you either sit in a room and don't come out, or you accept it, befriend it, and that's it."The affection among Ozzy's fans was apparent before the singer's funeral. Thousands of people lined the streets of Birmingham, laying floral tributes and singing Black Sabbath songs as Ozzy's body was transported through his home city in a hearse topped by a purple floral tribute in the shape of a cross.Sharon says he would have been mystified by the outpouring of love."He'd have been like, 'What's the matter with you guys? Go home!'" she says.But for the family, the public response was a huge source of comfort.Daughter Kelly said last year: "I never could have imagined it to be as helpful as it has been to know that we're not alone in our grief and our sadness, and that the rest of the world loved him as much as we did."Sharon says the fans' cards and messages were all collected, sorted and photographed; while the flowers were composted for the family garden, where Ozzy is buried."There was no way I could put Ozzy in a public graveyard," she says."I've seen what happens to other people in the public eye. There's no peace because people want to come and they want to pay their respects. That's an ongoing thing, and I wanted Ozzy to rest and just be."Does she visit him often?"Of course, every day. I can see him from my window."She still talks to him regularly, she says. Asked what she discusses, she puts a finger to her lips and gives a gentle "shh".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Ozzy's family - including children Jack and Kelly - stopped to read the tributes during his funeral procession last JulyOzzy and Sharon's relationship spanned more than 50 years. They met in 1970 and married in 1982. Their time together could be turbulent - he was arrested for attempting to murder her in 1989 (she dropped the charges), and they split briefly in 2016 amid rumours of infidelity - but the couple maintained that they were soulmates."It was an unusual relationship because we had such highs and such terrible lows," she admits. But at the end of his life, "he knew" how much he was loved.You can see proof of that love - from his family, his fans and his bandmates – in a new documentary about his final gig at Birmingham's Villa Park last year, when he reunited with heavy rock legends Black Sabbath.Titled Back To The Beginning, it features more than 25 of the songs played at that star-studded concert, including Ozzy's solo set and Sabbath's entire performance.In backstage footage, fellow A-list performers discuss the star's influence in awestruck tones."If there was no Sabbath, there's no Metallica," says the band's frontman James Hetfield. "It's as simple as that."Yungblud, whose version of Changes was one of the concert's emotional high points, talks about how, as a kid who didn't fit in, Ozzy changed his life."The fact he was celebrated for his madness and his individuality gave me hope."Figure caption, Watch: Black Sabbath blast out Iron Man at final gigSharon says the concert was Ozzy's final wish: the one thing that would make him happy after years of deteriorating health.But it almost never happened.Six months before the show, Ozzy fell and fractured his vertebrae. In recovery, he caught pneumonia three times. After surgery on his back, he caught sepsis and nearly died.Two weeks before the show, doctors urged him to call it off."They came to see us at the house and they said, 'You can't do this. We're advising you not to do this. Your heart's too weak'," Sharon recalls.But the singer was determined to see it through. In the film, it's hard to believe he's so ill. Although he performs seated on a throne, his eyes are full of life and his voice is powerful. As he looks out at the crowd, he seems elated.Backstage, Sharon admits, "the whole family was terrified". But something changed when Ozzy entered the stadium."He was sat in his dressing room, watching everybody on a screen performing, and he was like, 'I just can't believe they're all here'."It's amazing what support and love and determination can do for you, because [before the show] he was somebody that couldn't breathe. He had a lung condition. He had a heart condition. He had terrible, terrible agony from his spine. He had blood clots and he had Parkinson's."Some days just to even talk was an effort, let alone sing. And I don't know how he did it, but he did it."And you saw it in his eyes, in his face. It just made him feel like he was alive again."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ozzy is survived by Sharon, their three children (left-right: Kelly, Aimee and Jack) and three children from his previous marriageThe effect was so galvanising that, when he came off stage, Ozzy declared he wanted to go on tour."He was raring to go," Sharon laughs. "He was like, 'I can do this, and the fans don't mind if I'm sat down'."It's an incredible and rare thing, I suggest, to be able to grant your partner their last wish.Ozzy may have suffered immense pain in his final years, but he was able to say goodbye in style."To quote one of his songs, he was flying high again," Sharon says."He was just floating for those last 17 days. It was great. It was joyous."

schema.headline: Sharon Osbourne: 'I visit Ozzy's grave every day'

title: Manchester United & Michael Carrick: Air of inevitability around manager's future but owners' problems far bigger
description: There was an air of inevitability about Michael Carrick's walk around Old Trafford after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.It is not unusual for Carr
body: There was an air of inevitability about Michael Carrick's walk around Old Trafford after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.It is not unusual for Carrick to applaud the Manchester United fans. If anything, his acknowledgements were not as pronounced as they were in Como after the equally devastating loss.But after eight games without a win, the worst run since 2015-16 and two horrific defeats in a week, the end is approaching for Carrick, with his bosses in serious talks about his future.However, if anyone in a senior position at the club thinks the issues at Old Trafford will be solved simply by changing the head coach and, more importantly, the fans will be appeased by a new face in the dugout, the reaction from the stands on an awful day on and off the pitch would have very clearly told them otherwise.On Friday, as he looked back on that 4-1 loss to Como and ahead to Bournemouth, Carrick said: "We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."Sadly, they weren't.Carrick could not answer if he will still be in charge for next Saturday's trip to Chelsea. He does not know."The responsibility is mine," he said. "What else can I say really right now? I totally understand the situation. I'm not expecting anything either way. I love this place and I'll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club."The debt they initially landed on the club has now grown to over £1.15bn, according to their latest accounts. The amount it has cost in interest is £852m, according to respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble. In the last financial year, the interest payment was £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.The argument is, that money could have been used far more productively to sign better players.There had been hope Ratcliffe, a boyhood United fan, would change that when he struck a deal with the Glazers to become a minority shareholder on Christmas Eve 2023.Instead, a succession of decisions have led to major questions over his handling of the club.On the management side, United's hierarchy eventually backed Erik ten Hag after talking with alternatives in the wake of the shock 2024 FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City, spending over £200m on the likes of Leny Yoro, Matthijs de Ligt and Manuel Ugarte. Last week, Ten Hag told the Athletic, external the club went back on a promise not to sell homegrown Scotland international Scott McTominay to fund Ugarte's £50m move from Paris St-Germain. They sacked the Dutchman in October 2024.After that they persuaded Ruben Amorim to leave Sporting mid-season, when he wanted to wait until the summer.They stuck with him after an unprecedented 15th-place finish, and again after United lost to League Two Grimsby in the EFL Cup, then sacked him in January when he clashed with director of football Jason Wilcox over playing style.That led to Carrick's arrival to the end of the season, which turned into a permanent appointment after he guided the club back into the Champions League after a two-year absence.A third dismissal in three seasons would not reflect well on anyone.The 'Standards' banner that was held up on the Stretford End showing the images of legendary skippers Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and Roy Keane was there to remind the executives running the club of the history they should be aspiring to.Wilcox has largely operated behind the scenes but he could not fail to hear the obscenities being sung against him during today's game, nor the boos as he climbed into the vehicle taking him away from the stadium nearly two hours after the final whistle.Recruited from a similar role at Southampton following the Ratcliffe takeover and elevated in status following the dismissal of Dan Ashworth, amid the decision to recruit Amorim, the 55-year-old is blamed by many fans for the club's recent recruitment, even though the budget was set at a much higher level.Sat next to him at Old Trafford to watch the Bournemouth debacle unfold was chief executive Omar Berrada, who worked with Wilcox at Manchester City.Having senior figures steeped in City's recent history was always a potential problem if results didn't go well. Berrada played no part in the recent Premier League proceedings that found City guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, but the link is clear, and United's fans sang about that at Old Trafford as well.If that wasn't enough, a ticket touting investigation launched in the summer led to condemnation from all United's major fan groups. The club argued they were trying to catch touts, while fans felt it was an attempt to drive regular match-goers out in favour of more corporate sales. The club are adamant that is not the case, but the argument is falling on deaf ears.The same is also true of plans for a new 100,000-capacity stadium. The club conducted a survey which they said showed the majority of respondents were in favour of a new ground. The stadium is likely to cost in excess of £2bn and United spent £63.5m on land for it earlier this year.Some supporters simply don't believe those figures. The Stretford End impolitely told Ratcliffe they had no interest in a new stadium as well today.Carrick may take responsibility for poor results but there is far more than that causing unrest at Manchester United just now.

schema.headline: Manchester United & Michael Carrick: Air of inevitability around manager's future but owners' problems far bigger

title: Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally
description: Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republica
body: Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections."He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak.Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms.  Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday.Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency. In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins. El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan."We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said."She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added.Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj. "By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nicki Minaj. That's hard to miss."He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark.

schema.headline: Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally

title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
description: Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.Ending
body: Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.On the eve of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.The BBC understands the government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas and/or they will be offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.Some people may choose not to accept accommodation, but ministers say support will still be offered to them.The government said initial funding had seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks. Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.Ahead of hosting the summit, Burnham said: "Rough sleeping isn't a fact of life. It's a thing governments either choose to accept or don't."Well I don't accept it. That's why we're doubling funding so that people aren't just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this Parliament too."But we can't do it alone. If we're going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we're bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts."More than 30 organisations have pledged support for the plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities. Meanwhile, the National Housing Federation is working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use. However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."The Bed Every Night scheme Burnham set up while mayor in the region now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.He pledged to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester by 2020 when he came into power.When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021 but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.Across England, government figures show the number of people sleeping rough is at its highest level since records began in 2010.Lam continued: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises."Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices."Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."

schema.headline: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas

title: Brazil elections: Lula secures fourth term after dramatic comeback
description: Lula's campaign sprang back to life following his first-round defeat driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push.The former metalw
body: Lula's campaign sprang back to life following his first-round defeat driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push.The former metalworker, who has been the dominant figure on Brazil's left since he first ran for president in 1989, nevertheless faces the most challenging political landscape since first taking office in 2003.His new term, set to begin on 5 January 2027, will start amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.While Trump did not endorse Lula's rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, directly – something he did with the right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections held in Colombia and Honduras – there is little doubt his administration would have preferred to see a conservative at the helm of this country of 213 million people.The White House regards Latin America as an area of US influence with the Trump administration keen to have leaders in power who support its policies, including on defence, security and trade.It is also keen to reduce China's influence in the Western Hemisphere.Brazil, which is oil-rich and holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only big country in South America not governed by a right-wing leader, with Lula largely seen as China-friendly.Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to align Brazil more closely with Washington while Lula had warned the US not to interfere in the election and insisted that Brazil would "never fit into anyone's backyard".But while there may be disappointment in the White House, Lula's victory will be welcomed by environmentalists who had feared that a win by Bolsonaro would have given Brazil's influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power.They had pointed to record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during the presidency of his father, Jair, arguing that under the younger Bolsonaro laxer environmental policies could again lead to destruction in this key ecosystem.While Lula's supporters are ecstatic about his victory, the result shows that the country remains deeply divided, with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro.In addition to the challenge of uniting such a deeply polarised country, Lula will have to govern alongside the most right-wing Congress in Brazil's democratic era. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) was the party that made the biggest gains in the election.And yet, Lula's Workers' Party managed to organise huge rallies ahead of the run-off, showing the strong grassroots support it commands. Before the election, Lula had described the poll as "a parting of the waters for Brazil". He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil's opposing political poles with "a new way of governing", adding in a WhatsApp livestream before the election that "this country will never be the same again".While he provided little detail as to what the new way of governing would entail, he insisted he would "remain firm in the fight for a more just country, with opportunities for all and policies directed at the needs of the population".With a largely hostile Congress, this fight just may prove much harder for the veteran leadern - who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term - than in his three previous terms in office.

schema.headline: Brazil elections: Lula secures fourth term after dramatic comeback

title: Spotify uploads Irish lyrics for Dolly Parton's Welsh Jolene version
description: Image caption, Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene is the second posthumous release since her death in AugustByLeigh BoobyerBBC WalesThe lyrics to
body: Image caption, Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene is the second posthumous release since her death in AugustByLeigh BoobyerBBC WalesThe lyrics to Dolly Parton's Welsh version of her hit Jolene were uploaded mistakenly to Spotify in Irish.The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.The version has parts of the song sung in English and Welsh -  but the lyrics presented on the digital audio streaming service Spotify actually showed the language as Irish.Spotify removed the Irish lyrics after the BBC approached it for comment.The BBC asked Spotify when the single and lyrics were uploaded, when the error was noticed and when it will be replaced, but did not receive a response.Image caption, The lyrics on Spotify have been removed since the BBC approached the service for commentThe single came out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.The legendary country artist won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs after a career spanning seven decades.Jolene was released in 1973, and is about the fear she might lose her husband Carl Dean to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage.It was was nominated for a Grammy in 1974, gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60). It has since had more than one billion streams on Spotify, and many famous singers have gone on to cover Jolene.Image source, Bronwen LewisImage caption, Lewis and Star recorded their parts in the UK, while Parton recorded her parts in her studio in NashvilleThe Welsh version of the song came about after Lewis, from Neath, had translated the country classic and posted it on social media.Then Star, Parton's niece, reached out and suggested recording Jolene in Welsh with Lewis - and Parton joined too.In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd.Star revealed one side of the family from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens was initially believed to have come from Conwy.Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, in Powys, not Conwy as previously thought.

schema.headline: Spotify uploads Irish lyrics for Dolly Parton's Welsh Jolene version

title: Serbia's student movement: How and why students brought down Vučić
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Although it was a students' movement that won Serbia's election, no student has been electedByPaul Ki
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Although it was a students' movement that won Serbia's election, no student has been electedByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorTheirs is a movement born from tragedy that began with students blockading streets and turned into almost daily protests and a national movement against corruption and government negligence.In just under two years the students have succeeded in tearing up 14 years of political dominance under Aleksandar Vučić, who has seen support for his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) ebb away and ultimately fail in what became a referendum on the future of Serbia.From Belgrade to Novi Sad and Niš, the mood was euphoric as supporters gathered in town centres or in front of Student List headquarters. In a post on social media, the students declared "Serbia is free".Most symbolic of all was the demise of so-called Ćaciland, a pro-Vučić tent camp set up 18 months ago at Pioneers Park in central Belgrade in front of the Serbian parliament. Metal fences were torn down amid shouts of "Vučić is leaving".How the students changed SerbiaThey have no obvious leaders and have no grounding in politics, and yet the "Student List-Students Win" movement attracted anti-government voters across Serbian society.They fielded candidates for all 250 parliamentary seats, and yet no students were among them.As he joined the students marching towards Belgrade last week, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable.""We offer our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time," he told the BBC.It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.The tragedy was seen as emblematic of widespread corruption. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project."When the canopy collapsed that served as the last straw," says Helena Ivanov of the think tank the Henry Jackson Society. It was an emotional moment that triggered a spark and a national campaign of marches and events, she said, that captured the hearts and minds of Serbians in a way no opposition party had been able to do.From protests to direct challenge to VučićImage source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Aleksandar Vučić conceded victory, but said the students' movement would failWhat started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.Vučić's SNS was clearly shaken and by January 2025 his prime minister had resigned "to defuse tensions". In March 2025 Belgrade saw Serbia's biggest ever anti-government protest and as the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.By the time Vučić had announced snap elections last month, they were ready. "They have been able to take that emotional momentum into a proper organisation and have people learn how to protect fairness at polling stations," Helena Ivanov explained."The message was clear: the rule of law and not ruled by the law," said Gordana Delić, head of the Balkans programme at the German Marshall Fund of the US, who said Sunday's vote was in effect a referendum.Initially Vučić sought to praise the protesters as "well-intentioned", but ahead of the elections he accused them of trying to "bring down" Serbia. Even after conceding victory on Sunday night he made the unfounded allegation that they had the support of unnamed "European countries and the American deep state".Who will run Serbia now?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ilija Srdanović topped the Student List's candidates but is not seen as a likely prime ministerOne thing is clear, it will not be the students, as they were not standing for election. That was a calculated decision as the electorate would probably not voted for a list of candidates with little life experience.Although their top candidate was Ilija Srdanović, a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, he is not really seen as a likely prime minister. Few candidates stand out as potential leaders.At least 135 people on the list are thought to have won seats in parliament, and they include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga (24th on the list), renowned actor Tihomir Stanić (8th), opera singer Nikola Mikić (46th), former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić (27th), and a rather large number of professors.Šoškić's name has been mentioned in connection with the top post. He has spoken out about reforms he would make to the economy, and he has been widely criticised in pro-government media.What is their programme?The elected MPs will have the task of fulfilling what is in effect a manifesto.In the words of the students themselves, they were looking for people who could enter institutions "do their jobs responsibly and not forget why they are there".Under an 11-point programme, , externalthe student movement wants to:Eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for itPurge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crimeReform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political controlStop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises.Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.Will it still be a student movement, without students?Although they have not been elected, it is the students who have made the promises to the Serbian people and they will come under pressure to follow through on their manifesto.The ordinary Serbian citizens they chose to represent their movement have "been entrusted with transferring part of the struggle we have been waging on the streets for the past year into the institutions", the students say.In his speech on Sunday evening, Vučić told party supporters that the students had destroyed two years of life in Serbia and they would be defeated "faster than they think".

schema.headline: Serbia's student movement: How and why students brought down Vučić

title: Girl, four, dies after fall from tower block in Barking
description: A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in east London.The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an add
body: A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in east London.The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an address in St Paul's Road, Barking, at about 11:00 BST on Saturday morning, following reports that a child had fallen from height. Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service gave first aid and the child was taken to hospital, but later died from her injuries.A Met spokesperson said the incident was not believed to be suspicious."Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they said."An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious."We urge anyone with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 2424/24OCT."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook,, external X,, external and Instagram., external Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: British mum Leanne Gregory who died in Bahamas was celebrating wedding anniversary
description: Couple were celebrating anniversary before Bahamas tragedyImage source, SuppliedImage caption, Leanne and Nathan Gregory on their wedding dayByJodi La
body: Couple were celebrating anniversary before Bahamas tragedyImage source, SuppliedImage caption, Leanne and Nathan Gregory on their wedding dayByJodi Law and Ben CarrEast MidlandsThe husband of a woman who died as she tried to rescue her two sons when they were swept out to sea in the Bahamas said they had been celebrating their 10th wedding anniversary.Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been on a family holiday with husband Nathan when he believes their boys were swept into the ocean by a riptide.Although the children were rescued from the water on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.Speaking to the BBC on Sunday, Nathan, who is now back home with their sons, said the trip had been an early celebration for their anniversary in December.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Nathan said their relationship was perfectHe said both boys had been so excited and been snorkelling in shallow water as they sorted out their towels and bags on the beach when the boys got into difficulties.Both parents went into the sea and tried to save them as they were swept out by the current, he added, and the whole ordeal happened in less than 10 minutes.Nathan said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable", but she was a "hero... in life and in death" as she helped to rescue the two boys."I've known her since infant school," he told the BBC. "We first got together when we were 14... so 22 years.""There are no words I can use to describe Leanne, same as anyone she has ever known. "She was the purest of people, the most generous kind and beautiful person who ever walked the Earth."Our relationship was perfect. She was the perfect mother, the perfect wife, the foundation of our entire family."Nathan added: "Royal Caribbean and Virgin Airlines were absolutely incredible to us and made an impossible journey home so much easier."Now, as he "keeps strong for his boys", a fundraising page has generated nearly £9,000 in donations to support the family.Figure caption, Watch: Video provided by Nathan shows him taking a sunrise selfie in Miami one day before the tragedyMore tributes have paid to the family since the tragedy.Councillor Richard MacRae, who represents Stapleford north on Broxtowe Borough Council, said it was a "tight-knit community" that would rally around the family."It's sad, it's heartbreaking, when something tragic happens and people have got young kids involved, it is just a different level," he said."My thoughts and prayers are with the family and friends and the wider community."On a BBC Facebook post, people passed on their condolences.One post read: "Grateful to have known you and worked with you Leanne! "Gone too soon, but never forgotten."Stapleford Fire Station posted it was "deeply saddened" to hear of the mother of two's death.They said: "Our thoughts are with her family and friends at this difficult time."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Nathan said his wife loved the ocean and the whole holiday was based around that, sea life and nice foodThe two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas said.In a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given. Leanne was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected". A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas."We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Nottingham

title: Pierre Sage: Pressure grows as fans turn on Palace boss
description: "Oliver Glasner achieved some amazing things, and now I have to do the same," Pierre Sage said after replacing the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Euro
body: "Oliver Glasner achieved some amazing things, and now I have to do the same," Pierre Sage said after replacing the man who delivered an FA Cup, a European trophy and Community Shield during two years in charge at Selhurst Park.Four months into a three-year contract, the Frenchman is already under big pressure after a fifth defeat in eight Premier League games left the Eagles in the bottom four.Palace have failed to win their past four games and Sunday's 2-0 home defeat by Newcastle was greeted with boos from home fans, who had turned up hoping to see a positive response after last weekend's 5-0 humiliation at fierce rivals Brighton."There is no noise inside the club," said Sage when asked about his future in his post-match media conference."The boos are normal because we don't have the result."The noise is the consequence of the result of the team, and at the moment we don't have what we expect."Inside, we are just really focused on solutions. How to be better, how to create the conditions to compete, and we will continue our work, and there's no noise inside."Asked about boos from home fans during the match and at full-time, Sage accepted  it was an expected response after failing to win."It's normal that people lose patience when you lose, because everybody wants to win. Today it was not the case."Sage was named Ligue 1 manager of the year after leading Lens to a second-place finish as well as a French Cup triumph.But could time already be running out for the 47-year-old?Sage struck a defiant tone during his post-match media conference as he addressed questions about his future for 20 minutes."I don't have to convince the people around the club. I just have to convince the players to do their best to compete and to continue to improve," he added when asked further about his job."After that, this kind of decision is for the chairman, to the owners, this kind of person."For me, the noise around the team, the noise around the club, it's only noise."Palace have just seven points from their first eight league games in the post-Glasner era.After losing to Everton and Manchester City in their first two matches, Palace won at Fulham before losing at home to newly promoted Ipswich.They secured a rare clean sheet in a goalless draw at Leeds before coming from behind to beat Nottingham Forest at Selhurst Park on 11 October.That was their last win. They have since lost at his former club Lyon in the Europa League, and Brighton, before drawing 2-2 against Besiktas in Istanbul on Thursday.However, patience is clearly wearing thin after fans reacted to the latest defeat by Newcastle.In addition, Palace have the worst defensive record in the Premier League after conceding 19 goals in eight games. Their next Premier League match is at improving Tottenham next Saturday, before hosting Liverpool on 8 November going into the international break. Palace's first game back is at fellow strugglers Coventry City on 21 November.Will Sage still be in charge by then?French football expert Julien Laurens said Sage needed to be more ruthless."He's a lovely guy. He's maybe a little bit too nice at times," Laurens, speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, added."Remember when Crystal Palace beat Fulham earlier in the season? That was Palace's first win of the season and he felt sorry for Fulham. "You don't feel sorry in this league. This Premier League is ruthless. It's the top, top level. This is the best league in the world. "You can't feel sorry for the opposition you have just beaten, especially when this is your first win and you needed it badly. "But this is the kind of guy that he is."Sage's Lens side were built on aggressive pressing and a willingness to attack quickly once they won the ball back.The Opta numbers showed a team intent on regaining possession high up the pitch. Lens made 426 high turnovers during the 2025-26 season, frequently turning those moments into chances - producing 69 shots and seven goals.However, Palace are clearly struggling to fire under Sage's leadership."He needs to do things slightly differently," added Laurens. "There is pressure everywhere in the Premier League."Former Manchester United and England forward Dion Dublin said Sage needed to be tougher if he is to have a long-term future at Palace."It's no good being lovely with everything," added Dublin, also speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live."Things can't be lovely when you are a Premier League manager. You will just lose games and get sacked."Former Leeds United forward Lucy Ward told 5 Live: "He has proved himself at Lyon and Lens. Being a little bit too nice doesn't help."

schema.headline: Pierre Sage: Pressure grows as fans turn on Palace boss
